invidious

in-VID-ee-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Invidious is likely to cause resentment or ill will, often through an unfair comparison.

Splitting the family inheritance equally among five siblings with very different needs put the trustee in an invidious position.

Example

The teacher faced an invidious choice: publicly naming only one 'most improved' student when three of them had worked equally hard all semester.

Invidious describes a situation that unfairly favors one person over equally deserving others, breeding resentment through no fault of anyone involved.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unfair: Unfair means not treating everyone justly, and it covers anything from a biased rule to a bad call. Invidious is narrower and more loaded: an invidious task or comparison is unfair in a way that almost guarantees resentment against somebody.

resented: Resented describes something people already feel ill will toward -- the damage is done. Invidious looks forward instead: an invidious choice or comparison has not been resented yet, but its unfairness makes that ill will nearly certain to come.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enviable: desirable and worth having

equitable: fair and unbiased

Where it sits · how much bad feeling it stirs

awkward → invidious → repellent

awkward vs. invidious: Calling a situation merely awkward undersells it; invidious specifically implies the awkwardness comes from unfairness that breeds real resentment.

repellent vs. invidious: Repellent goes further than invidious, describing something so unfair it provokes outright disgust, not just quiet resentment.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: against, into (Latin)

root — vid: to see (Latin (videre))

suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together: in- ('against') + vid ('to see') + -ious together trace back to 'looking at with ill will' -- the resentment-provoking quality invidious now describes.

Use the root in a new word: video: Video comes from the same Latin root videre ('to see'), the same vid- buried inside invidious.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Invidious almost always describes a situation, task, or comparison -- not a person's character directly.
